headline: Rotation, not a rout: money is leaving AI tech for health care, financials and staples, and the equal-weight index is beating the cap-weighted one
summary: Over the past month the S&P 500 (SPY) fell about 2% while the equal-weight index (RSP) rose about 3%: a 5-point gap that shows how narrow the damage is. Technology (XLK) is down 10% in a month and 16% from its high after the sharpest one-day drop for the sector in over six years, with chips swinging hard around Nvidia. Health care (+6.6%), staples (+6.5%), financials (+6.2%), discretionary, utilities and real estate all rose. Behind it: a hawkish Fed (a December hike is fully priced and the 10-year is at 5.14%), doubts about who funds the AI build-out, and oil near $88 on the Iran war.
drivers: AI-infrastructure doubts hit the largest sector

Tech is about 34% of the index (rolled forward from about 40% in early October), so its slide drags SPY even when most stocks rise. The worries are about funding and payback, not demand: questions over neocloud contracts, Nvidia financing its own customers, and export-control headlines. Q3 earnings for the sector still grew 69% (FactSet), which is why the forward P/E has fallen to 17.3, its lowest since March 2020 and below the market's for the first time since 2017.

October PPI was 6.5% year on year and Fed officials are talking about hikes; the 10-year yield rose to 5.14% and the dollar is at its highest since April 2025. That hurts long-duration growth stocks and rate-sensitive yield proxies alike, but helps bank net interest margins.
Defensives with earnings growth are the winners

Money is going to sectors that hold up in selloffs but still grow: health care has the best 6-month return (+31%) and drew $2.1bn into XLV in a month, while XLF sits within 1% of its 52-week high. Staples rallied to a 52-week high too, but that is a defensive bid on a 23.7x forward P/E, not an earnings story.
Energy is cheap but losing momentum

Energy earnings grew about 149% in Q3 on Iran-war oil prices and the sector trades at 11.7x forward earnings, the lowest of any sector. But crude fell about 2.5% last week after the IEA flagged a Q4 supply surplus, and XLE is down 2.4% over the month with RSI in the mid-30s.
rotation: The rotation map shows how lopsided the move is: tech has fallen into Lagging and energy has rolled from Leading into Weakening, while eight of the other nine sectors sit in Leading, simply because tech's slide lifts everything else relative to SPY. Communication services is the exception, still below the line but Improving. Rotations like this tend to run for weeks, not days. The historical tell for a turn is tech stabilising while its inflows continue, and that is what the flow data shows now: investors are still buying XLK (+$2.2bn in a month) even as it falls. Watch for XLK reclaiming its 50-day average (about 9% above the price) after Nvidia's results on Nov 17.
flows: State Street creations and redemptions (shares outstanding × NAV) show dip-buying in tech (+$2.2bn into XLK over a month, +$3.6bn over 3 months) and steady inflows into health care (+$2.1bn in a month). Financials are the big outlier: XLF has lost $4.0bn over 3 months even as prices hit 52-week highs. Investors are under-owned into the rally, which is constructive if the rotation lasts. Utilities lost $1.6bn in a month: the AI-power trade is being unwound as data-center delays mount. SPY took in $7.5bn in a month, so money is staying in equities, just changing seats.
model: The model score blends six z-scored factors across the 11 sectors: 12-1 month momentum (25%), 3-month return relative to SPY (20%), trend versus the 200-day average (15%), 1-month ETF flows as % of assets (15%), forward P/E relative to the S&P 500 (15%, lower is better) and latest-quarter earnings growth (10%). It ranks energy first (cheapest valuation, fastest earnings growth, best 12-month momentum) and health care second (best 3-month relative strength and trend). Utilities, communication services and industrials rank last. Tech sits mid-table: strong 12-month momentum, valuation and earnings offset the worst 3-month relative strength of any sector. Where my stance differs from the model (energy neutral, financials overweight), the cards explain why.

idx.src: FactSet Earnings Insight, Nov 6, 2026 (P/E as of Nov 5)

weightsSrc: Schwab Center for Financial Research, as of Oct 2, 2026; rolled forward by each sector ETF's price change

XLV.view: The cleanest leadership in the market: the best 6-month return of any sector, steady ETF inflows and earnings that don't depend on the economy or on AI capex. It is a defensive sector that is also growing, which is exactly what a market facing Fed hikes wants.
XLV.modelView: Ranks second overall, with the best 3-month relative strength (about +16 points vs SPY) and the strongest trend of any sector (about 18% above the 200-day), backed by inflows. The weak spots are stretch (RSI near 70) and only mid-single-digit earnings growth, so the expected return from here is lower than the last six months.
XLV.trade: Hold the overweight; add on a pullback towards the 50-day average rather than chasing at RSI 70.
XLV.risk: Drug-pricing or policy headlines, and a sharp tech rebound that pulls money back out of defensives.

XLF.view: A 5%+ 10-year yield and a steeper curve support bank margins, capital-markets activity is strong, and the sector trades at 15x forward earnings, about 85% of the market multiple and below its long-run relative average. XLF is within 1% of its 52-week high.
XLF.modelView: Mid-table (about 4th): solid trend (about 9% above the 200-day) and positive relative strength, held back by flows. XLF has seen about $4bn of redemptions over 3 months while rising. The model scores that as a negative, but I read it as a contrarian positive: the rally isn't crowded, which is why my stance is above the model's.
XLF.trade: Overweight; prefer large money-centre banks and brokers over regional banks if credit spreads widen.
XLF.risk: Private-credit or commercial real estate losses, and a sharp curve flattening if the Fed over-tightens.

XLK.view: Price momentum is broken (down 16% from the high, 9% below the 50-day) but the fundamentals are the best in the index: 69% earnings growth, 94% of companies beat, and a forward P/E below the market's for the first time since 2017. Positioning is already washed out (Deutsche Bank has tech exposure below April 2025 lows) and the ETF is still taking in money.
XLK.modelView: Mid-table overall. It has the second-best 12-month momentum and scores well on valuation and earnings, but the worst 3-month relative strength of any sector (about −8 points vs SPY) and a trend sitting right on the 200-day average. A momentum trader would wait and a value investor would buy. The flow factor (steady creations through the drawdown) tips it to accumulate rather than avoid.
XLK.trade: Build back towards benchmark weight in thirds: one after Nvidia's Nov 17 print, one on a close back above the 50-day average, one on a retest of the low that holds.
XLK.risk: AI funding stress spreading from neoclouds to hyperscaler capex guidance; a higher-than-expected December dot plot.

XLP.view: Staples led Friday's session and are at a 52-week high, but this is a safe-haven bid, not an earnings upgrade. At 23.7x forward earnings they cost 34% more than the market while growing far slower, and they compete with 5% Treasury yields.
XLP.modelView: Strong on 3-month momentum and trend, weak on valuation; flows have been negative ($0.2bn out in a month). Investors are rotating in through single stocks, not the ETF.
XLP.trade: Neutral; use strength to trim into health care, which has a similar defensive profile with more growth.
XLP.risk: A deeper growth scare would extend the defensive bid further.

XLE.view: The cheapest sector (11.7x) with the fastest earnings growth (about 149% in Q3) thanks to Iran-war oil prices, and it is still up 48% this year. But the oil tape is turning: the IEA sees a Q4 surplus, WTI fell about 2.5% last week, and XLE has lost momentum.
XLE.modelView: Ranks first in the model: top of the valuation, earnings and 12-month momentum factors. But the short-term trend is rolling over (RSI mid-30s, down 2.4% over the month, now Weakening on the rotation map) and flows are flat. That is why I hold it at neutral rather than following the model's overweight: the score is backward-looking and the oil tape has turned. It works as a hedge against a geopolitical oil spike, less so as a core overweight.
XLE.trade: Hold at neutral as a portfolio hedge against Middle East escalation; don't add until crude stabilises.
XLE.risk: A ceasefire or OPEC+ supply could knock $10–15 off crude; escalation is the upside risk.

XLB.view: Materials have quietly done well (+17% this year) on copper, gold and data-center materials demand, and the sector posted about 30% Q3 earnings growth. Volume-based money flow is the strongest of any sector, but it is a small sector (under 2% of the index) and sensitive to the strong dollar.
XLB.modelView: Middle of the pack overall; the 20-day Chaikin money flow (volume-based buying pressure) is the strongest of any sector, and ETF flows are small and mixed.
XLB.trade: Neutral; prefer gold and copper miners over chemicals while the dollar is strong.
XLB.risk: A stronger dollar and slower China demand.

XLC.view: The sector is down about 7% this year and below its 200-day average as investors question the return on Meta's and Alphabet's AI spending, even though Q3 earnings grew 14% and analysts see about 35% upside to targets. At about 18x forward earnings it is no longer expensive.
XLC.modelView: Near the bottom: flat 12-month momentum, below its 200-day average and the second-worst flow score ($0.6bn out in a month, about 3% of assets). Valuation is the only positive.
XLC.trade: Neutral; a bounce candidate if tech turns, but it needs to reclaim its 200-day average first.
XLC.risk: More capex increases without matching revenue; advertising slowing if the consumer weakens.

XLI.view: Industrials fell 9% over three months as the AI-power and data-center equipment trade unwound, and the sector still trades at a premium (21.7x) to the market. Higher rates and a strong dollar also weigh on machinery and exporters.
XLI.modelView: Weak on 3-month relative strength and trend (below the 200-day); valuation is a negative factor. Flows are roughly flat.
XLI.trade: Underweight; keep aerospace and defence (supported by the war) but avoid electrical-equipment names priced for uninterrupted AI build-outs.
XLI.risk: A fast tech and AI-capex rebound would lift the electrical-equipment names first.

XLY.view: Discretionary bounced 6% this month but is roughly flat over a year, trades at 24.3x forward earnings, and is dominated by Amazon and Tesla. Higher mortgage and card rates squeeze lower-income consumers.
XLY.modelView: Low 12-month momentum and a poor valuation score; the 1-month bounce has improved relative strength but flows are still negative.
XLY.trade: Underweight; fade the bounce, using October retail sales (Nov 17) as the next test.
XLY.risk: A strong holiday season or a Tesla-specific rally.

XLU.view: Utilities rallied 6% this month on the defensive rotation, but a 5.14% 10-year yield competes directly with their dividends, and the AI power-demand story is being questioned as data-center projects slip. XLU lost $1.6bn in redemptions over the month.
XLU.modelView: Overbought (RSI about 70) with weak 12-month momentum; outflows give it the worst flow score of any sector.
XLU.trade: Underweight; use the bounce to reduce.
XLU.risk: A bond rally if the Fed turns dovish, or a sharp risk-off move.

XLRE.view: Real estate is the most rate-sensitive sector and the Fed is still talking hikes. Data-center and health-care REITs are the exceptions; office and retail face refinancing at much higher rates.
XLRE.modelView: Mid-table: positive short-term relative strength and money flow, but weak 12-month momentum and no valuation input. ETF flows are small.
XLRE.trade: Underweight the sector; prefer data-center and health-care REITs if exposure is needed.
XLRE.risk: A fall in long yields would spark a sharp short-covering rally.

The swing factor for tech (37% of the index) and for the AI-capex chain in industrials and utilities; retail sales test the discretionary bounce.

AI server demand and margins; the export-control overhang.
A hike is fully priced; the dot plot decides whether financials keep leading and whether rate-sensitive sectors (utilities, real estate) stay under pressure.
XLK vs its 50-day average; XLF flows
Tech reclaiming its 50-day average while still taking in money would signal the rotation is ending; XLF flows turning positive would confirm financials' leadership.
